news_drafts.headline: East Dunbartonshire health and social care partnership running down reserves to cover funding shortfall
news_drafts.lead: The Health and Social Care Partnership serving East Dunbartonshire has depleted nearly a third of its general reserves in a single year to bridge a funding gap, with savings targets falling far short of what is needed. The partnership achieved only 39 per cent of its 2026/27 savings programme by month 4, a shortfall it is covering by drawing down £8.192m from reserves. General contingency reserves have fallen from £3.955m to a projected £1.290m by March 2027. The partnership explicitly warns that continued reliance on reserve drawdowns to balance budgets "may be compromised" its financial sustainability. The financial strain has forced service access restrictions: charges are rising, eligibility criteria tightening and waiting lists extending. A 3.5 per cent pay uplift for staff was approved with no corresponding funding, adding to the pressure. The partnership carried forward £3.036m in unachieved savings from previous years, which must still be realised alongside current targets.

news_drafts.headline: East Dunbartonshire underlying borrowing need to reach £785m by 2028/29, cash reserves to fall to £1.7m
news_drafts.lead: East Dunbartonshire's underlying borrowing need, the total the council has spent on long-lived assets it has not yet paid for, will grow by 39 per cent over three years to £785m by 2028/29, according to the council's treasury management strategy. The council is currently using cash balances to bridge the gap between what it owes and what it needs to borrow. However, that buffer will shrink by 94 per cent, from £27.6m to £1.7m by 2028/29, as capital spending on housing and other programmes accelerates. Once reserves are exhausted, the council will need to borrow for all new capital expenditure. The forecast reflects a sharp increase in housing investment, with Housing Revenue Account capital spending peaking at £86.4m in 2027/28, more than five times the £16m spent in 2024/25.

findings.headline: The Capital Strategy on this agenda indicates future costs where borrowing is extended, with those pressures met from Council Tax.
findings.detail: The paper says significant decisions on the new Capital Strategy have yet to be taken. It notes that debt charges increase where borrowing is extended, with those pressures met from Council Tax as the legislative backstop.
findings.matters: A finance director reads a council's future debt-charge exposure, and whether Council Tax meets it, as the core test of whether borrowing is affordable.
findings.quote: where borrowing is extended and debt charges are increased with these pressures being met from Council Tax

findings.headline: Officers continue to restrict expenditure to business critical items across all areas of Council business, without exception.
findings.detail: The paper says virements are approved where resources flow from underspending areas to areas where overspending is unavoidable, and not where the aim is to enhance expenditure levels. Exceptions include grants and redeterminations.
findings.matters: Spending controls and virement rules are what a finance director at another council looks for when a council is managing an in-year overspend.
findings.quote: Officers continue to restrict expenditure to only business critical expenditure across all areas of Council business, without exception.

findings.headline: The Council has raised cash flow risk over year-end redeterminations with other Directors of Finance and COSLA.
findings.detail: The paper says increasing commitments are funded through year-end redeterminations, and the Council wants funding provided through the year, matched to service delivery. Redeterminations amalgamated into the 2026/27 budgets include Scottish Disability Payments and Breakfast Clubs.
findings.matters: Funding that arrives at year end rather than matched to spend is a cash flow exposure a finance director at another council will recognise.
findings.figures: Scottish Disability Payments £0.406m; Breakfast Clubs £0.344m; Children's Social Care uplift £0.263m; Targeted Revaluation £0.215m
findings.quote: With increasing commitments funded through year-end redeterminations, the Council has raised risks in relation to cash flow

findings.headline: In-year council tax collection was 46.03% at August 2026, a 0.18% decrease on the previous year.
findings.detail: The paper says the collection rate has marginally decreased in recent years and that increased payments in February and March make predictions harder. Debt recovery processes are to be stepped up as resources allow.
findings.matters: In-year collection is the early signal a finance director uses to judge council tax income, and the paper says forecasting it is becoming harder.
findings.figures: 46.03% in-year collection rate at August 2026; 0.18% decrease on the previous year
findings.quote: in-year collection rates for August 2026 equated to 46.03%, a 0.18% decrease from that reported in the previous year.

findings.headline: The debt charges budget includes a £5.975m capital grant mitigation, which the paper describes as a temporary measure in the 2026/27 budget.
findings.detail: The paper says debt charges depend on borrowing levels, terms and interest rates, and tend to follow the capital programme. It reports a projected debt charges variance of £0.000m.
findings.matters: A finance director will want to know how a temporary mitigation of this size is replaced in later years, since debt charges follow the capital programme.
findings.figures: £5.975m capital grant mitigation; £0.000m projected debt charges variance
findings.quote: The current debt budget reported includes a capital grant mitigation of £5.975m. This is a temporary measure included in the 2026/27 budgeted position.
